Compromise Of 1850. The Compromise of 1850 was a series of legislative measures that temporarily defused the crisis over slavery's expansion into western territories acquired from the Mexican-American War. Crafted by Henry Clay and negotiated through bitter sectional debate, it admitted California as a free state, organized new territories without slavery restrictions, and included a draconian Fugitive Slave Act compelling northern compliance with slavery enforcement. Though hailed as a triumph of compromise, it intensified sectional hostility and postponed rather than resolved the conflict that would erupt in civil war eleven years later. California's admission as a free state disrupted the sectional balance: the Senate had maintained equal numbers of free and slave states since the Missouri Compromise (1820); California's entry threatened Southern dominance. Henry Clay, the "Great Compromiser," orchestrated the package: California free; New Mexico and Utah organized as territories with popular sovereignty (voters would decide slavery); the slave trade (not slavery) abolished in Washington, D.C.; and a harsh Fugitive Slave Act (1850) passed. The Fugitive Slave Act required northern citizens to assist in capturing enslaved people; it overrode state laws and denied fugitives trial by jury; its brutality shocked northerners and radicalized abolitionists who saw it as proof of slavery's tyranny. Daniel Webster, a northern senator, surprised many by supporting the Compromise, declaring "I wish to make myself heard, not as a New England man, but as an American"; his "Seventh of March" speech endorsed the package but damaged his reputation among abolitionists. Southern secessionists like John C. Calhoun rejected the Compromise as insufficient; Calhoun opposed California's admission and any curb on slavery expansion, foreshadowing Southern grievances that would justify secession in 1861. The Compromise briefly calmed sectional tensions but created new flashpoints: enforcement of the Fugitive Slave Act sparked resistance in northern states; the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) undid the territorial provisions, reigniting conflict.
